method: priceIndex: World Bank ICP 2021 price levels relative to the US (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/sources/90, PX.WL) for three categories that stand in for preparedness goods: food, furnishings and household equipment, and machinery and equipment. Food and household goods are consumer prices that include US sales tax, so they are multiplied by 1.02 and 1.07 (Tax Foundation's 7.53% average combined rate, https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/state/sales-tax-rates/, with groceries mostly exempt); equipment prices exclude VAT on both sides, so they are multiplied by 1 + the local standard VAT or GST rate (recalled), which a household pays. The geometric mean of the three is the 2021 index against US pre-tax prices. It is moved to November 2026 by the change in the consumption price level from 2021 to 2025 (WDI PA.NUS.PRVT.PP and PA.NUS.FCRF, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/indicator/PA.NUS.PRVT.PP; GDP PPP for Argentina, which has no consumption PPP after 2021), relative CPI from the 2025 average to October 2026 (OECD, https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.SDD.TPS,DSD_PRICES@DF_PRICES_ALL,1.0, US 1.048; news reports of the official releases for Argentina, Turkey and Nigeria; assumed for countries whose OECD series stops in December 2025) and market exchange rates on 20 November 2026 (https://open.er-api.com/v6/latest/USD, matching the ECB reference rates of 19 November). micromortValueUsd: 14.6 x (Atlas GNI per capita 2025 / US 88,810) (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.CD, updated 11 November 2026), income elasticity 1; lo is the lower of 0.466 x mid (the HHS low/central ratio) and the elasticity-1.5 transfer; hi is the higher of 1.53 x mid (HHS high/central) and a transfer by GNI per capita at PPP. timeValueUsdPerHour: the HHS method (median hourly earnings less income tax and employee contributions) applied to each country: Eurostat SES 2022 medians (https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/earn_ses_pub2s) uprated by the Eurostat wage cost index (lc_lci_r2_a) for the EU and EFTA; ILOSTAT median hourly earnings (https://rplumber.ilo.org/data/indicator/?id=EAR_EHRM_SEX_CUR_NB_A) or national releases elsewhere, uprated to November 2026; tax rates from OECD Taxing Wages 2025 (https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.CTP.TPS,DSD_TAX_PIT@DF_PIT_AV,1.0, mean of the rates at 67% and 100% of the average wage); converted at 20 November 2026 rates; then multiplied by 0.967 so that the same steps applied to the US (ILOSTAT/CPS median $26.80 in 2025) give the anchor's $21. Lo is half the mid and hi 1.7 times it (1.9 for figures resting on snippets or bridges), as in the anchors.

reproduced.basis: The formula applied to the US itself gives 1.03: ICP prices include US sales tax, which the model's US item prices leave out. The preset is 1 by definition and stays 1.

anchors.comment: Matches the preset up to the US sales tax, which the definition excludes for the US only.

reproduced.basis: Population-weighted mean of the 17 Western European countries below (Germany 1.04, France 1.03, UK 1.02, Italy 0.98, Spain 0.97, Netherlands 1.05, Switzerland 1.33, Norway 1.31, Denmark 1.20 and others).

anchors.comment: 1.03 against the preset's 1.10 (0.90-1.35), inside its range. The preset was a judgment with no prices fetched; the dollar is also about 3% stronger against the euro than its 2025 average (EUR 0.911 per USD on 20 November 2026).

reproduced.basis: Argentina by the same formula: ICP 2021 food 0.70, household goods 0.77, equipment 1.43, with VAT 21%: 1.00; real appreciation since 2021 (GDP PPP 38.8 to 567.3, CPI to October 2026 1.43, ARS 95 to 1,563 per USD) x1.21.

anchors.comment: 1.22 against the preset's 1.4 (1.0-2.3), inside its range. The preset leaned on a cross-border import (a Sawyer filter at five times its US price); ICP's comparable-product prices put the typical good lower. Item-level overrides would remain better than one index.

reproduced.basis: Identity: the transfer starts from the HHS 2026 VSL ($14.1M central, $6.6M low, $21.5M high in 2025 dollars, x1.035) used by the preset.

anchors.comment: Reproduced exactly; the ranges for other countries scale the same low/central and high/central ratios (0.466 and 1.53).

reproduced.basis: Population-weighted Atlas GNI per capita 2025 of the same 17 countries, $53,300, / US $88,810 = 0.60; x14.6 = 8.8.

anchors.comment: 8.8 against the preset's 7 (3.5-11). The preset's mid was the geometric middle of the income transfer (8.5) and older official European values ($4-5M); the brief's method (elasticity 1, Atlas GNI) gives the transfer alone. Either the preset should rise toward 8.8 or the country figures should carry the same discount; I did not apply one.

reproduced.basis: Argentina: Atlas GNI per capita 2025 $14,650 / $88,810 = 0.165; x14.6 = 2.41. Lo: elasticity 1.5. Hi: GNI at PPP $31,920 / $89,490 x 14.6 = 5.2.

anchors.comment: National 2.4 against the preset's 3.0 for the city of Buenos Aires, whose mid included a city income premium (about 1.25); the national range matches the preset's 1-6 closely.

reproduced.basis: ILOSTAT median hourly earnings 2025 (CPS) $26.80 x1.051 (wage growth to November 2026) x (1 - 0.229, OECD rate) = $21.7.

anchors.comment: The worker-based CPS median with the OECD tax rate gives $21.7 against HHS's $21.0 (job-based OEWS median $24.43 with 17% tax). All countries are multiplied by 21.0 / 21.7 = 0.967 so the US equals the anchor.

reproduced.basis: Population-weighted mean of the 17 Western European country figures below (15.1 without Switzerland).

anchors.comment: 15.6 against the preset's 15 (7.5-26): the preset used the same SES medians but an assumed USD 1.15 per EUR, against 1.098 now, and a flat 29% tax. (Checker: units corrected; the text read 'EUR 1.15 per USD'.)

reproduced.basis: Argentina: EPH median hourly take-home pay 2025 ARS 5,192 (31 urban areas) x1.42 to November 2026 / 1,563 x 0.967 = $4.6.

anchors.comment: National urban 4.6 against the preset's 5.5 for the city of Buenos Aires, where wages are about 20% above the urban average; consistent.

openQuestions: Hardship dollars (FEMA and other US willingness-to-pay figures) are not scaled by country, while the micromort value and time value now are. In India the micromort value is 0.45 against 14.6 in the US, so an unmet day of water at $85 weighs about 30 times more against death there than in the US. Scaling hardship by the same income ratio would keep the trade-off between hardship and death the same everywhere.

The westernEurope preset micromort value (7) is below what the brief's method gives for Western Europe (8.8), and the preset price index (1.1) is above it (1.03). Countries with their own figures and countries falling back on the preset will therefore differ by about 20% on the VSL for reasons that are not about them. Align the preset or accept the gap.

Official VSLs differ a lot from the income transfer for some countries: Australia A$5.87M (US$3.9M, against the transfer's 10.5), the UK about GBP 2M (unverified, about 2.6). If the model should use official national values where they exist, these would fall by 60-75%.

The micromort values for the poorest countries depend mostly on the income elasticity: at 1.5 (Robinson, Hammitt and O'Keeffe's reference case for low- and middle-income countries) India and Nigeria fall five- to seven-fold. The lo values carry that case.

The time value uses each country's median earnings of employees, as the HHS method does. In countries where most work is informal or self-employed (India, Indonesia, Nigeria, the Philippines), the employee median may overstate what the typical adult's hour is worth; it may also understate it for the urban middle class who are the likely readers.

One price index cannot capture the gap between local generic goods (cheap in China, India, Nigeria) and branded imports (dear in Argentina, Brazil, Turkey). An index for staples and one for imported equipment, or item-level prices, would be better.
